newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Regretful Taiwan challenges S.Africa's China move.
newsitem.headline: Regretful Taiwan challenges S.Africa's China move.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday it regretted South Africa's decision to switch diplomatic ties to Beijing but held out hope the move might be reversed.

"This action seriously hurts the friendly relationship between the two countries," Foreign Ministry spokesman Peter Cheng told reporters. "For this extremely unfriendly decision we express our regret."
President Nelson Mandela said on Wednesday South Africa would shift recognition to Beijing from Taipei over the space of a year, with completion by the end of 1997.
Cheng indicated that Taipei felt the decision was not final, calling on Pretoria to reverse it and vowing to seek new talks.
"The South African government should cherish the friendly relationship between the two countries and seriously reconsider this decision," he said.
The news, which caught Taipei off guard, would not undermine Taiwan's resolve to break free of diplomatic isolation imposed by its communist rival in Beijing, he said.
"This case definitely will not affect our determination to actively develop international space," Cheng said.
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, and has steadily won diplomatic allies with its demand that countries choose Beijing or Taipei.

The move strips the exiled Republic of China government of its biggest diplomatic ally and will leave the Nationalist-ruled island recognised by only 29 states -- mostly poor countries in Central America and Africa that depend on Taiwan for aid.
Experts said it reflected a weakening of Taiwan's position after Beijing and Washington eased some of their differences in Sunday's summit of presidents Bill Clinton and Jiang Zemin.
"This is another major blow for Taiwan and the pragmatic diplomacy promoted by President Lee Teng-hui after the Clinton-Jiang meeting," said National Taiwan University political scientist Tim Ting.
"The policy has cost us our last major diplomatic ally. Communist China is demonstrating to Taiwan that it has too many bargaining chips besides military power," Ting said.
A Western diplomat in Beijing said South Africa's move could have ripple effects.
"This will reduce the remaining coterie of diplomatic partners for Taiwan," he said. "And other smaller African countries might follow suit."
Officials of Taiwan leaders had taken succour from Mandela's recent remarks that it would be "immoral" to abandon Taiwan.
Until Wednesday, Mandela had resisted intense pressure from Beijing to drop Taipei and recognise the People's Republic of China, saying he wanted good relations with "both Chinas".
Mandela's two China formulation is heresy to Beijing, which reserves a right to use force to bring Taiwan under its rule.
While the political pain to Taiwan will be acute, there may be an economic cost for South Africa, where plans for a US$3.5 billion Taiwan-financed petrochemical complex could collapse.
South Africa's Taipei ambassador, Johannes Viljoen, told Reuters he hoped Taiwan would not exact economic reprisals.

"Of course they are a very important trading partner of South Africa, our sixth largest, and also an important source of assistance," he said by telephone. "We sincerely hope the projects they have going in South Africa would continue."
Nearly 300 Taiwan businesses have operations in South Africa with investments topping US$1.5 billion.
Yet South Africa also covets huge new markets in China, where bilateral trade has soared in the 1990s.
In 1995, exports to China doubled to one billion rand ($231 million) -- less than half of its exports to Taiwan, which grew to 2.5 billion rand ($577 million).
